newsitem.title: SWEDEN: ATHLETICS-KIPKETER FINALLY MATCHES COE'S 800 WORLD RECORD.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-KIPKETER FINALLY MATCHES COE'S 800 WORLD RECORD.

text.p: Wilson Kipketer came agonisingly close to breaking the oldest world track record on Monday when he equalled Seb Coe's 16-year-old 800 metres mark at the Stockholm Grand Prix.
Seemingly off the pace when the field went through the bell in 49.22 seconds, Kipketer emerged with 200 to run and appeared to gather strength as he raced down the home straight.

At the line the time was given as one minute 41.74 seconds -- 0.01 of a second outside Coe's mark. But even as Kipketer was jogging his victory lap, the time was adjusted down and the Kenya-born Dane had a share of the world record.
"I am a little bit relieved," Kipketer said. "Because now nobody's going to ask about the world record again."
Kipketer emigrated to Denmark in 1990, was ranked world number one in 1994 and raced away with the world title in Gothenburg in the following year.
Following protests by the Kenyan Federation he was not allowed to compete for Denmark at last year's Atlanta Olympics but was still the world number one with five successive times under 1:42.

He broke the world indoor record twice at the Paris world championships in March and was clearly set to mount a serious assault on a mark which has defied the best two-lap runners in the world since 1981.
He said he had never come across Coe but added: "I would like to meet him one day."
Three times world steeplechase champion Moses Kiptanui, who had not trained since the middle of last month through illness, failed in a valiant bid on his own world record earlier in the meeting.
But his time of 8:01.80 was still the third fastest in history and only the Kenyan himself has ever run faster.
Moroccan Hicham el Guerrouj, just half a second outside Noureddine Morceli's world mile record in Oslo on Friday, was again a disappointed man.
El Guerrouj clocked 3:29.30 seconds over 1,500, outside Morceli's world mark. But it was the fastest time of the year and only Morceli has ever run faster.
"I was very disappointed for the second time in four days," said el Guerrouj. "Over the final 200 metres I suddenly felt very tired."
"Up to now it's the best day of my life. I do not feel lucky, I feel satisfied, as long as I do my best I feel satisfied with what I am doing."
One man clearly delighted with his night's work on a sweltering Scandinavian evening at the venue which staged the 1912 Olympics was Trinidad's Ato Boldon.
Boldon, bronze medallist in both the 100 and 200 in Atlanta, won the 100 in 9.95 seconds and followed with victory in the 200 in 19.82 seconds, fastest this year and sixth fastest of all time.

Boldon, who trains with the American 100 champion Maurice Greene, said the pair were planning to reduce the world record from 9.84 to 9.7 or 9.6 seconds and predicted fast times at next month's Athens world championships.
"Athens is going to be even better than Atlanta in terms of times," he said.

The impressive American 100 champion Marion Jones won the women's 200 in a year's best of 22.16 and there was another year's best for Slovenia's Igor Kovacs who clocked 13.13 with a following wind of 1.6 metres in the 110 metres hurdles.
Despite the string of world class performances in the penultimate grand prix before the world championships, the most popular man of the night was nine times Olympic champion Carl Lewis.

Lewis, sporting a new hairstyle which gave him a passing resemblance to former French tennis champion Yannick Noah, anchored the Santa Monica Track Club to victory in the 4x100 relay and was still signing autographs in the infield well after the meeting had finished.
